name: Jacques Chirac
summary: Chirac was a Gaullist-descended centre-right president who combined market-oriented tax and privatisation policies with defence of pensions by répartition, social protection and the French model of laïcité. His own speeches stress Europe, a multipolar world run through the UN, aid and the environment, an independent nuclear deterrent, and abolition of the death penalty.
notes: Rules 7, first pass. Sources read: the library's 28 Elysee and vie-publique texts (1995-2006 statements, interviews and campaign programmes, in French), the 35 EUSpeech 2007 speeches (machine translations of his own French texts), the UN General Debate and Security Council speeches, Universalis chapters and the 1986 privatisation entry. Themes searched by keyword in French: death penalty, nuclear deterrence and energy, UN and force (Iraq 2003), Europe, euro and sovereignty, laicite and the school headscarf law, Vel d'Hiv and Holocaust denial, aid, climate and the Charte de l'environnement, referendums and institutions, decentralisation, privatisation, pensions, taxes, deficits, immigration, crime, abortion, same-sex unions, euthanasia, drugs, guns, family, GMOs. No Chirac text on abortion, same-sex unions, euthanasia or drugs was found in the library, so those stay null. Where the sources hold only a procedural or partial remark (conscription reform, mandatory sentences, the 2005 state of emergency, illegal-immigration control, the 0.7 percent aid pledge's financing) no statement is settled and the answer is null. Laws promulgated on his government's initiative (loi 2004-228, loi 2003-775) are not used as his own record; his positions come from his speeches. Two readings are borderline: force-without-un rests on his 2003 UN speech and Iraq statements (France's 1999 Kosovo participation is not in the library); public-ownership rests on the 1986 privatisation record (he also kept EDF public in 2002). Failing the uncertainty rule on the pluralism/authoritarianism and class lines is the honest result: he made no statement on one-party rule, opposition, media control or class struggle.
